content: The initial studies on the use of dried blood spots (DBS) for hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA testing date back over 20 years, but only recently have additional studies been conducted to explore this area further. While systematic reviews have been published on HBV diagnostics and the use of DBS, no systematic review specifically addressing the diagnostic accuracy of HBV DNA testing using DBS exists to date. Recent reviews on DBS in hepatitis C virus (HCV) RNA testing and tropical diseases did not include data on the diagnostic accuracy of HBV DNA in DBS. Existing guidelines for HBV management focus on treatment eligibility, initiation of first-line therapies, switching treatments, and monitoring, but they do not include recommendations for screening. The World Health Organization (WHO) is currently developing guidelines for testing chronic HBV and HCV infections in lowand middle-income settings. These guidelines will consider the potential use of DBS for serological and molecular testing of HBV and HCV to improve access to and uptake of testing. To support the development of these guidelines, this systematic review evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of HBV DNA testing using DBS compared to serum samples. The review aims to assess the sensitivity and specificity of DBS for HBV DNA detection. The research question developed for this purpose is: Among individuals undergoing HBV DNA testing, what is the diagnostic accuracy and impact of detecting HBV DNA from DBS samples compared to venous serum samples? The review included observational and interventional studies that compared HBV DNA testing in DBS with serum as the reference standard. Only English-language studies were included, and no restrictions were placed on participant demographics or geographic location. The target conditions were HBV diagnosis, patient follow-up, and treatment monitoring. Sensitivity was defined as the proportion of true HBV infections detected by DBS testing, while specificity referred to the proportion of negative results in DBS testing confirmed by serum testing. Correlation and regression coefficients were also analyzed to assess the relationship between HBV DNA levels in DBS and serum. The search strategy involved databases such as MEDLINE, Web of Science, EMBASE, Global Health, and LILACS, with the search conducted in August 2015. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened using predefined eligibility criteria. Data extraction focused on study characteristics, including author, publication date, country, participant demographics, type of specimen, storage conditions, and diagnostic performance metrics. Statistical analysis was performed using STATA 13, employing bivariate analysis for sensitivity and specificity when more than four studies contributed data. Forest plots were used to assess heterogeneity, and likelihood ratios were calculated from pooled sensitivity and specificity. The review identified 485 abstracts, of which 48 full-text articles were assessed for inclusion. Ultimately, 10 studies were included in the qualitative review, and eight studies contributed to the quantitative analysis. Among these, four studies provided data for both sensitivity and specificity estimates. The included studies originated from Europe, Africa, Asia, and Mexico, with no data from children and limited demographic reporting. Most studies used whole blood for DBS preparation, except one that used plasma. The diagnostic accuracy of HBV DNA testing in DBS showed sensitivity ranging from 93% to 100% and specificity ranging from 86% to 100%. Pooled bivariate analysis revealed an overall sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 100%, though the latter had wide confidence intervals. Univariate analysis of seven studies yielded a pooled sensitivity of 97%. However, no guidelines exist for the use of HBV DNA assays on DBS, and studies have tested the detection limits of these methods. Detection limits for serum assays ranged from 10 to 100 IU/mL, with a cutoff of 20,000 IU/mL. Storage conditions did not significantly affect diagnostic accuracy, as studies storing DBS samples at temperatures ranging from 4°C to 37°C for up to seven days reported no decline in performance. However, all pooled results are valid only under the tested storage conditions, which may limit applicability in field settings. Stratified analysis by assay type (in-house vs. commercial) showed similar sensitivities (95% and 98%, respectively). The quality of included studies was generally low, with a high risk of bias. Many studies did not adequately report sampling methods or participant flow, and none blinded laboratory personnel to the reference or index tests. Four studies were downgraded due to case-control designs, and five studies lacked sufficient reporting on sampling. This resulted in a high overall risk of bias and low-quality evidence. The review highlights the scarcity and suboptimal quality of data on the use of DBS for HBV DNA testing. While sensitivity compared to serum is good, specificity estimates are imprecise, and storage conditions do not unduly affect DBS performance. However, the limited number of studies, small sample sizes, and lack of individual-level data restrict the ability to draw robust conclusions. Future research should focus on larger, well-designed diagnostic accuracy studies that test DBS under real-world storage and transport conditions and report clinically relevant detection thresholds. Additionally, meta-analyses of individual-level data from published and unpublished studies could provide more comprehensive insights.
